topic: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Reflection of waves (physics only)
subject: physics

items.q: A wave travelling through the air reaches the surface of a still pond. Which statement about reflection is correct?
items.correct: Some of the wave is reflected at the boundary between the air and the water.
items.misconception: No reflection happens here, because reflection needs a polished mirror surface.
items.why: Almost every example met before GCSE is a mirror, and the everyday word 'reflection' means the image you see in one. Sound reflects from a cliff to give an echo, ultrasound reflects inside the body, and light reflects from a still pond. What matters is a boundary between two different materials, not a mirror.
items.random_wrong: Reflection happens only if the wave travels from the water into the air.

items.q: A walker shouts towards a cliff face and hears an echo a moment later. What has happened to the sound wave?
items.correct: It has been reflected at the boundary between the air and the rock.
items.misconception: It has been absorbed by the rock, which is why the sound returns later.
items.why: 'Absorb' and 'reflect' are both used loosely in everyday speech about sound, and students know soft furnishings change the sound of a room without being sure which way round. An echo is reflected sound returning from a hard boundary. Soft, porous materials absorb sound energy instead of returning it, which is why a carpeted room sounds dead and a bare hall sounds echoey.
items.random_wrong: It has been transmitted through the rock and out of the other side.

items.q: A black matt surface is left in bright sunlight and becomes noticeably warm. Which statement best explains this?
items.correct: Light is absorbed at the surface and the energy is transferred to a thermal store.
items.misconception: Light is absorbed at the surface, so the energy carried by the wave is destroyed.
items.why: The wave really does stop, and nothing can be seen or heard afterwards, so it looks as though the energy has gone. Energy is never destroyed. A black surface left in sunlight absorbs the light and becomes measurably warmer, which is where the energy has gone.
items.random_wrong: Light is transmitted through the surface and carries its energy out the far side.

items.q: A ray of light travels from air into a thick glass block. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: It is transmitted into the glass, travelling at a different speed from before.
items.misconception: It is transmitted into the glass with its speed and its direction both unchanged.
items.why: A window looks perfectly clear, so it seems that the light must pass through without anything happening to it. A ray entering a glass block at an angle is visibly bent, which shows the speed of the wave has changed at the boundary. The clear view through a window is because the two bends, going in and coming out, cancel each other for parallel faces.
items.random_wrong: It is absorbed at the boundary, so no light gets into the glass at all.

items.q: In a ray diagram for reflection, the angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and which line?
items.correct: The normal, the line drawn at 90° to the surface at the point of incidence.
items.misconception: The surface itself, at the point where the incident ray strikes the mirror.
items.why: The surface is the obvious line in the diagram and is already drawn, while the normal has to be added by the student, so it feels like an optional extra. The two angles add up to 90°, so a ray at 30° to the mirror has an angle of incidence of 60°. Always draw the dashed normal first and measure both angles from it.
items.random_wrong: The reflected ray, taking the whole angle between the two rays together.

items.q: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror. The angle between the incident ray and the mirror surface is 30°. What is the angle of reflection?
items.why: The surface is the obvious line in the diagram and is already drawn, while the normal has to be added by the student, so it feels like an optional extra. The two angles add up to 90°, so a ray at 30° to the mirror has an angle of incidence of 60°. Always draw the dashed normal first and measure both angles from it.

items.q: A student draws a ray diagram of light reflecting from a plane mirror. Which feature shows that the diagram is correct?
items.correct: The two rays are on opposite sides of the normal, with their angles to it equal.
items.misconception: The two rays are on the same side of the normal, with their angles to it equal.
items.why: Students learn 'the angles are equal' as the whole of the law, and equal angles can be drawn on either side of the normal without breaking that rule. The ray has to travel away from the surface on the far side of the normal, or it would be going back along its own path. Draw the incident ray, the normal, and then the reflected ray as its mirror image in the normal.
items.random_wrong: The angles to the mirror surface are equal, so no normal needs to be drawn.

items.q: Thick curtains and a carpet are put into a bare room, and echoes in the room become much quieter. Which statement explains this?
items.correct: The soft materials absorb more of the sound, so less of it is reflected back.
items.misconception: The soft materials reflect the sound much better than the bare hard walls did.
items.why: 'Absorb' and 'reflect' are both used loosely in everyday speech about sound, and students know soft furnishings change the sound of a room without being sure which way round. An echo is reflected sound returning from a hard boundary. Soft, porous materials absorb sound energy instead of returning it, which is why a carpeted room sounds dead and a bare hall sounds echoey.
items.random_wrong: The soft materials transmit all the sound straight out of the building.

items.q: Standing in a lit room at night you can see the street outside a window and a faint reflection of yourself in it. What does this show?
items.correct: Reflection, transmission and absorption can all happen at the same boundary.
items.misconception: Only one of reflection, transmission or absorption can happen at a boundary.
items.why: The three words are taught as three separate cases, and diagrams normally show only one ray, which suggests only one outcome is possible. At a window you can see the street through the glass and a faint reflection of yourself in it at the same time, while the glass itself warms slightly in the sun. All three are happening at that one boundary.
items.random_wrong: All of the light is transmitted, and the faint image comes from the air itself.

items.q: In the required practical a narrow ray of light is shone first at a plane mirror and then at a sheet of white paper. What is seen?
items.correct: The mirror gives one clear reflected ray; the paper scatters light in many directions.
items.misconception: The mirror gives one clear reflected ray; the paper reflects no light back at all.
items.why: Students use 'reflection' to mean 'making an image', so a surface with no image in it seems not to be reflecting. You can only see the paper because light reflects off it into your eyes. The surface is rough, so the normals point in many directions and the reflected rays are scattered instead of staying together.
items.random_wrong: Both give one clear reflected ray, but the paper reflects at a much larger angle.

items.q: In the refraction part of the practical, a narrow ray passes from air into a glass block at an angle to the normal. What happens as it enters?
items.correct: It slows down and changes direction, bending towards the normal.
items.misconception: It carries straight on without bending, whatever the angle of incidence.
items.why: Refraction is remembered as 'light bends in glass' rather than as a change of direction that depends on the angle of incidence. At an angle of incidence of 0° there is no sideways difference across the beam, so there is nothing to turn it. The ray goes straight on, more slowly, and is still refracted in the sense that its speed has changed.
items.random_wrong: It slows down and changes direction, bending away from the normal.

items.q: The same ray reaches the far face of the glass block and passes back out into the air. What happens as it leaves?
items.correct: It speeds up and bends away from the normal as it enters the air.
items.misconception: It speeds up but bends towards the normal, as light always does.
items.why: The first example students meet is air into glass, where the ray bends towards the normal, and that single case gets remembered as a rule. The direction of the bend follows the change of speed. Slowing down, as in air into glass, bends the ray towards the normal; speeding up, as in glass into air, bends it away.
items.random_wrong: It carries on along the same line it followed inside the block.

items.q: Why does a ray of light change direction as it passes from air into a perspex block?
items.correct: The light travels at a different speed in perspex than it does in air.
items.misconception: The light bends around the edge of the block as it passes the corner.
items.why: The bend is seen at the edge of the block, so the edge looks like the cause, and 'bending round things' is a familiar everyday idea. The direction changes at the flat face, wherever on that face the ray enters, and not at the corners. It is the change of wave speed at the boundary that changes the direction.
items.random_wrong: The perspex absorbs some of the light, and absorbing it turns the beam.

items.q: In the practical a ray is aimed along the normal at the flat face of a glass block. What is observed?
items.correct: The ray carries straight on without bending, though its speed does change.
items.misconception: The ray bends towards the normal, as it does at every angle of incidence.
items.why: Refraction is remembered as 'light bends in glass' rather than as a change of direction that depends on the angle of incidence. At an angle of incidence of 0° there is no sideways difference across the beam, so there is nothing to turn it. The ray goes straight on, more slowly, and is still refracted in the sense that its speed has changed.
items.random_wrong: The ray carries straight on and keeps exactly the same speed in the glass.

items.q: AT 4 and AT 8 concern observing how waves interact with matter. Which technique makes the angles measured in this practical most reliable?
items.correct: Use one narrow slit in the ray box and mark each ray with two dots set well apart.
items.misconception: Use the widest and brightest beam available so that each ray is easy to see.
items.why: Faint rays are genuinely hard to see in a bright lab, so students open the slit or use several slits to make the beam obvious. A wide beam has no single path, so the pencil line and the angle both become uncertain. Use one narrow slit and dim the room instead, and mark the ray with two dots as far apart as possible.
items.random_wrong: Measure the angle inside the block by holding the protractor against the glass.

items.q: A student investigates how much glass, perspex and water each bend a ray of light. Which variable must be controlled for the comparison to be valid?
items.correct: The angle of incidence, kept the same for each of the three substances tested.
items.misconception: The angle of incidence, changed for each substance so that more data is collected.
items.why: Students know more readings are usually better, and confuse collecting a wide range of data with controlling a variable. If two things change at once you cannot tell which caused the difference. Fix the angle of incidence for every substance; a range of angles can be investigated separately with one substance.
items.random_wrong: The width of the beam, made as wide as possible for each substance in turn.

items.q: Does the law of reflection hold for a rough surface?
items.correct: Yes. Every single ray obeys it; the surface roughness makes the normals point in different directions.
items.misconception: Rough surfaces break the law of reflection, so light comes off them at bigger angles than it went in.
items.why: Scattered light looks disorderly, and a rule that produces order seems not to apply where the result is disordered. Zoom in on a rough surface and each tiny facet is flat and tilted differently. Each facet reflects its own ray at an angle equal to its own angle of incidence, and the many different normals send the rays in many directions.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How do you find the path of the ray inside a glass block?
items.correct: Mark where it enters and where it leaves, remove the block, and join the two points.
items.misconception: You have to measure the ray inside the block, so you hold the protractor against the glass and read it off there.
items.why: The refracted ray is visible inside the block, so it seems natural to measure it while the block is still in place. The block cannot be drawn on and the protractor cannot sit flat on it. Draw round the block first, mark the entry and exit points, take the block away, and join the marks to reveal the path inside.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
